items.title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Optimizing Energy Consumption in Power Distribution Networks
items.abstract: Abstract With the continuous growth in electricity consumption and the increasing penetration of renewable energy sources, power distribution networks have become more complex in terms of both structure and dynamics. The operational efficiency of these networks plays a crucial role in ensuring a reliable and cost-effective energy supply. Traditional network control and management methods often lack the capability to respond promptly to fluctuations in demand and generation. This paper proposes a hybrid artificial intelligence-based framework for optimizing energy consumption in power distribution networks. In the proposed approach, the load demand at different network nodes is initially predicted using artificial neural networks. Subsequently, an optimization algorithm, such as a genetic algorithm or reinforcement learning, is employed to adjust the network configuration and schedule distributed energy resources. Simulation results on the IEEE test system demonstrate that applying this approach can significantly reduce power losses and improve voltage stability. The findings indicate that the proposed intelligent system, by improving load forecasting accuracy and optimizing network scheduling and configuration, can substantially reduce energy losses. items.title: Artificial Discursive Intimacy: A Relational Formation in the Age of Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Companions
items.abstract: The proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots has given rise to a novel form of human–AI intimacy, yet its fundamental nature remains undertheorized. Drawing on a dialogical perspective, this study conceptualizes human–AI chatbot relationships as “artificial discursive intimacy” (ADI), a distinct relational formation in which intimacy is constituted through discourse with a disembodied algorithmic interlocutor, moving beyond the paradigm of human-to-human mediated intimacy. Based on in-depth interviews with 29 AI companion users, we identify four key differences between ADI and human discursive intimacy, including a shift from absent to activated presence, from reciprocity to unilaterality, from uncertainty to predictability and precarious safety, and from alterity to multi-dimensional mirroring. To understand how users navigate the ontological gap between human and AI, we propose a quadrant framework mapping human and AI social capabilities. This reveals dual animation processes of anthropomorphic animation, in which users project human embodied qualities onto AI, and robotomorphic animation, in which users internalize AI's machine-generated discursive patterns as relational ideals. Our findings suggest that ADI is sustained by a recursive interplay of these processes, with implications for how intimacy, relational selves, and human connection are being fundamentally reshaped in the age of AI.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND AI-ENABLED ROBOTIC PROCESS AUTOMATION IN THE LEGAL SYSTEM: CONCEPTUAL FOUNDATIONS OF ELECTRONIC LEGAL PERSONALITY
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) and robotic process automation (RPA) is transforming the technological environment in which legal relations arise and are implemented. Unlike traditional automation based primarily on predetermined rules, AI systems can analyse large volumes of data, identify patterns, generate predictions, adapt their behaviour and select among alternative outputs. This creates new challenges concerning legal attribution, liability, contractual relations and intellectual property. The article examines the relationship between AI and RPA from legal, technological and inter- disciplinary perspectives, with particular attention to the relationship between technological auton- omy and legal personality. It argues that technological autonomy cannot, by itself, constitute grounds for granting an AI system legal personality, since legal personality is a normative construct estab- lished by law. The relevant question is whether a special legal status would provide an effective response to specific regulatory problems. The study distinguishes conventional automated information systems, AI systems that assist human decision-making, and highly autonomous AI systems. While traditional legal mechanisms may generally be sufficient for conventional automation, AI-assisted and highly autonomous sys- tems require additional safeguards concerning transparency, traceability, human oversight and accountability. The article also examines the informational structure of AI and the need to distin- guish hardware, software, algorithms, models and data in relation to property rights, intellectual property and liability. The concept of electronic personality is analysed in the context of the contemporary European approach, particularly Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), which establishes a risk-based framework focused on safety, fundamental rights, transparency and human oversight. For Ukraine, the article proposes a gradual regulatory model based on coherent terminology, risk- based classification, transparency, traceability, human oversight and clear liability rules. Further regulation should address automated contractual activity, AI-generated results and risk insurance. A special electronic legal status should be considered only after sufficient technological, legislative and judicial practice has demonstrated that existing legal mechanisms are inadequate.

items.title: Artificial intelligence anxiety, academic engagement, and academic burnout among Chinese music students: a cross-sectional study across educational levels
items.abstract: Objective To examine educational-level differences in artificial intelligence (AI) anxiety, academic engagement, and academic burnout among Chinese music students, and the independent associations of AI anxiety with the two academic outcomes after adjusting for relevant covariates. Methods This cross-sectional study included 1,168 music students from 14 Chinese universities across eight provinces and municipalities (824 undergraduates, 276 master’s students, and 68 doctoral students). Welch’s ANOVA, multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA), adjusted general linear models, and hierarchical multiple regression were used to examine group differences and associations. AI anxiety × educational-level interactions were also tested. Results Adjusted educational-level effects were small (partial η 2 = 0.017 for AI anxiety, 0.011 for academic engagement, and 0.012 for academic burnout; multivariate partial η 2 = 0.008 for engagement and burnout jointly). Adjusted comparisons showed differences among all three educational levels in AI anxiety. Undergraduates reported lower academic engagement than both postgraduate groups. For burnout, undergraduates scored higher than master’s students, while the undergraduate–doctoral difference was not significant. AI anxiety correlated negatively with academic engagement ( r = −0.166) and positively with academic burnout ( r = 0.361). After adjustment, AI anxiety remained negatively associated with engagement ( β = −0.141) and positively associated with burnout ( β = 0.332). Neither association varied significantly across educational levels. Conclusion Educational-level differences in AI anxiety, academic engagement, and academic burnout were small. AI anxiety was independently associated with both academic outcomes, with no significant moderation by educational level. These findings highlight the importance of considering students’ psychological experiences when integrating AI into higher music education.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in critical care: A narrative review on promise, progress, and challenges
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming critical care medicine by enabling data-driven clinical decision- making, early disease prediction, and personalized patient management. With the increasing complexity of intensive care and growing shortages of trained critical care specialists, AI has emerged as a promising tool to improve diagnostic accuracy, optimize resource utilization, and support timely therapeutic interventions. This narrative review critically examines the current evidence regarding the applications, benefits, challenges, and future directions of AI in critical care. A focused literature search of PubMed, MEDLINE, Scopus, and Google Scholar was conducted, prioritizing English-language publications, expert consensus statements, systematic reviews, and clinically relevant original studies published between 2015 and 2026. Current evidence indicates that AI has demonstrated substantial potential in early prediction of sepsis, acute kidney injury, and clinical deterioration, while enhancing personalized decision support, intensive care unit triage, workflow optimization, nutritional management, and antimicrobial stewardship. However, the available literature is predominantly based on retrospective observational studies and machine-learning model development, with limited prospective validation and few randomized clinical trials evaluating patient-centered outcomes. Major barriers to widespread implementation include data heterogeneity, limited interoperability, algorithmic bias, lack of model transparency, ethical concerns, regulatory uncertainty, and inadequate external validation. Despite these limitations, AI has considerable potential to augment, rather than replace, clinician expertise by supporting evidence-based decision-making and improving healthcare efficiency. Future research should emphasize multicenter prospective validation, explainable AI, standardized reporting, ethical governance, and implementation science to facilitate safe, equitable, and clinically effective integration of AI into routine critical care practice.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education: Rethinking Curriculum, Assessment, and the Role of the Teacher
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how learners access information, practise skills, receive feedback, and demonstrate understanding. These developments create an opportunity to reconsider curricula that place disproportionate emphasis on recall, but they do not make foundational knowledge or memorisation obsolete. This perspective article argues that schools should integrate AI as a means of strengthening inquiry, critical evaluation, creativity, problem-solving, and ethical judgement while preserving the human relationships and disciplinary knowledge on which learning depends. Drawing on selected literature and a practitioner reflection from an international-school context in Angola, the article proposes a curriculum-oriented approach organised around four connected priorities: competency-focused learning objectives, assessment redesign, educator development, and explicit AI literacy. It also considers risks involving unequal access, unreliable outputs, privacy, bias, academic integrity, and over-reliance. The school-based reflection is presented as an illustrative account rather than a formal evaluation, because systematic outcome data are not reported. The article concludes with practical recommendations for school leaders, teachers, policymakers, and accreditation bodies. Responsible integration requires more than access to tools: it requires clear governance, equitable provision, informed professional judgement, and assessment practices that make students’ thinking visible.

As a result, English language teaching is gradually moving from traditional teacher-centred instruction toward more flexible and learner-centred models.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Mental Health Referral and Documentation: An Analysis of Clinician Reflections
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) and automation become embedded across the continuum of mental health care, their influence is increasingly felt not only in therapeutic encounters but in the infrastructural processes that surround them. Aim This paper explores how technology-based referral platforms and AI-assisted documentation address two major barriers to care: delays in access and the stigma of seeking mental health or substance use services. Method This study employed a qualitative, exploratory design to examine how clinicians perceive and respond to artificial intelligence (AI) assisted referral and documentation tools within mental health and social work practice. Results Analysis of practitioner reflections revealed three overarching themes: 1) perceived benefits and workflow improvements, 2) ethical ambivalence and concerns around consent, and 3) clinical identity and resistance to automation. The themes illustrate the complex landscape clinicians navigate when adopting AI-based documentation tools. Conclusion Clinicians’ reflections on AI are not merely technical. They are deeply tied to questions of professional identity, relational ethics, and the nature of evidence-based practice. This study highlights the need to reframe AI not as a replacement for clinical reasoning or narrative complexity but as a potential ally, one that must be thoughtfully designed and governed.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Public Administration: Delegation of Functions, Responsibility, and Legitimation Practices
items.abstract: The article examines the process of the artificial intelligence (AI) systems implementation into the structures of public administration focusing on the actual distribution of the powers of authority, the problem of accountabil-ity, and discursive legitimation practices. Based on a qualitative comparative analysis of four international cas-es (Romania, China, the USA, the UK), it is established that the AI systems primarily perform information pro-cessing functions and routing tasks, without replacing a human at the stage of final political decision-making. The study proves that the public presentation of the AI is often used by authorities as a legitimation tool to demonstrate competence, impartiality, and technological modernity even when the actual role of the algorithm is limited. It is concluded that the prospects of total algocracy do not yet give cause for concern as the AI activity is still incorporated in the current mechanisms of power and serves only to renew officials’ institutional reputa-tion.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN RECRUITMENT: EFFECTIVENESS, RISKS AND ETHICAL LIMITATIONS
items.abstract: The article examines the effectiveness, risks, and ethical limitations of artificial intelligence (AI) in recruitment. A distinction is made between deterministic automation, algorithmic systems, machine learning, and generative AI, which makes it possible to avoid equating any digital HR tool with artificial intelligence. Based on a systematized review of recent academic literature, comparative and content analysis, as well as analysis of regulatory documents, the evidence regarding the impact of AI on recruitment performance is synthesized. It is shown that the strongest evidence concerns operational effects: the ability to process large volumes of applications, automate repetitive tasks, support sourcing, screening, matching, and communication, and reduce recruiters’ workload. At the same time, the evidence is substantially less conclusive with respect to quality of hire, candidate experience, and the elimination of bias. The article analyzes algorithmic bias, indirect discrimination, opacity, false exclusion of qualified candidates, privacy and information-security risks, automation bias, and the potential dehumanization of recruitment. Particular attention is paid to meaningful human oversight and to the current regulatory framework, including the EU AI Act, the GDPR, and Ukrainian legislation. An author-developed matrix for assessing the appropriateness of AI use in recruitment is proposed. It combines the expected effect, strength of evidence, discrimination and privacy risks, severity of potential error, and the required level of human oversight. Three modes of AI use are substantiated: automation-preferred, AI-assisted decision-making, and human-led decision-making. The principle of proportionality between automation and risk is formulated, according to which the permissible autonomy of an AI system should decrease as the potential harm of an algorithmic outcome increases.

items.abstract: This study examined artificial intelligence (AI) utilization, associated classroom challenges, and academic performance among Senior High School students at Tigao National High School, Surigao del Sur, Philippines, during the Academic Year 2025-2026. Employing a mixed-methods research design, the study involved 122 respondents comprising 107 students and 15 teachers. Quantitative data were gathered through questionnaires and pretest–posttest assessments and analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and paired-samples t-tests, while qualitative data were examined through thematic analysis. Findings revealed that respondents demonstrated functional ICT literacy (M = 3.72) and frequently utilized AI for research, writing assistance, and academic activities. Academic performance increased from a pretest mean percentage score of 60.76% to 65.42% in written assessments and 79.53% in oral assessments, with statistically significant differences (p < .05). ICT literacy demonstrated a significant positive relationship with academic performance (r = .52, p < .05). Qualitative findings identified unreliable internet connectivity, limited devices, academic integrity concerns, and excessive AI dependence as persistent challenges. The study concluded that responsible AI integration, strengthened digital literacy, and appropriate instructional safeguards are essential to supporting academic achievement and equitable technology-enhanced learning.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy and Public Acceptance of AI Technologies among Adults in Iraq
items.abstract: This study investigated the relationship between Artificial Intelligence (AI) literacy and public acceptance of AI technologies among adults in Iraq. The role of AI in public services, healthcare, education, banking, and digital communication is growing, making it a key sociological and policy issue to understand what factors affect citizens' acceptance of AI. A quantitative cross sectional survey design was used and data were gathered from 420 adults living in Iraq. Artificial Intelligence literacy and public acceptance of AI technologies were measured by a structured questionnaire with a five-point Likert scale. The data were analysed by descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, exploratory factor analysis, Pearson correlation and regression analysis using IBM SPSS Statistics software. The results showed that the participants had a moderate to high level of AI literacy and moderate levels of public acceptance of AI technologies. The Pearson correlation analysis showed that there was a statistically significant positive correlation between the concepts of artificial intelligence literacy and public acceptance. The regression analysis also revealed that AI literacy was a significant predictor of public acceptance, accounting for 32.0% of the variance, and multiple regression analysis indicated that AI literacy is the most significant predictor, even after controlling for demographic and technology-related characteristics. The study is a significant contribution to the sociology of artificial intelligence, as it illustrates how AI literacy is a crucial social resource that influences citizens' receptivity to new technologies. The results highlight the need to encourage AI literacy initiatives to foster informed public acceptance and facilitate responsible digital transformation in Iraq.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-enabled updating and application of guideline-based algorithms for symptom management in adults with cancer: a concordance evaluation of cancer-related fatigue, depression, and pain
items.abstract: Introduction Cancer-related fatigue, depression, and pain are highly prevalent, often co-occur and impair physical function, social activities, and quality of life among adults with cancer. Despite the availability of evidence-based clinical guidelines that provide recommendations for assessment and management, these symptoms remain under-recognized and undertreated. Clinical decision support systems (CDSS) can operationalize guideline-based symptom management algorithms at the point of care. However, maintaining these systems as evidence and practice evolve is labor-intensive, limiting adoption and sustainability. To address this gap, we sought to evaluate an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled approach to updating guideline-based algorithms and generating patient-specific recommendations for managing fatigue, depression, and pain among adults with cancer. Methods This study evaluated AI performance (Gemini 3.0 Pro) for two tasks: identifying and interpreting updates to cancer symptom management guidelines for fatigue, depression, and pain, and producing casespecific recommendations aligned with an existing rule-based CDSS. Guideline updates were assessed against expert-judged reference standards using an ordinal rubric for detection, completeness, accuracy, and safety. Vignette-based recommendations were compared using precision, recall, and F1-score at the level of discrete clinical recommendation elements. Results For guideline updating, AI performance met pre-specified acceptability thresholds for fatigue and pain, with high completeness and accuracy and no clinical safety risk. Performance for depression was variable, driven by omission of guideline-supported integrative therapies and non-specific pharmacotherapy guidance. In vignette analyses, AI-generated recommendations showed strong concordance with the rule-based CDSS (F1 0.86–0.96). Most mismatches between AI and the CDSS came from AI leaving something out, not from giving unsafe advice. Discussion This suggests AI currently works best as a support tool rather than making clinical decisions on its own. Broader clinical use will require further work to test a greater number of test vignettes and its performance in real-world, multi-site settings with diverse patient populations.

items.title: Assessing individual differences in teachers' proactive behavior: insights into the reliability and stability of high and low inference measures
items.abstract: Despite growing interest in teachers as agents of change, research lacks a coherent framework for studying teachers' initiatives to improve their school environments. Drawing on research in organizational psychology, the present study investigates two complementary measurement approaches to assess teachers' proactive behavior, defined as self-initiated actions to enhance school functioning and facilitate organizational improvement: first, teaching-specific adaptations of three established high-inference scales intended to capture different types of proactive behavior (voice, taking charge, and personal initiative), and second, a newly developed low-inference behavior checklist. Using two samples of German teachers (N EarlyCareerSample = 165, N Cross − AgeSample = 130), we demonstrate that the instruments assess proactive behavior reliably, are substantially interrelated, and show the expected associations with the established constructs organizational citizenship behavior and work engagement. Evidence for the distinctiveness of voice, taking charge, and personal initiative was stronger in the Early Career Sample than in the Cross-Age Sample, where the dimensions showed considerable overlap. The behavior checklist captures a broad range of concrete proactive actions and is strongly related to all three high-inference measures. Beyond introducing instruments for assessing proactive behavior in teachers, the findings reveal meaningful variation across teachers, schools, and over time, support the empirical distinctiveness of proactive behavior from organizational citizenship behavior, and demonstrate its positive association with work engagement.

items.title: Assessing the safety and vulnerability of educational systems against disaster risks using the SAVES tool
items.abstract: Extreme weather and climate events impacted schools serving approximately 242 million students in 85 countries in 2024. Despite growing recognition of schools’ role in disaster risk management, the literature lacks integrated methods to assess schools’ exposure to water-related hazards, school building conditions, and the organizational capacities of educational systems to ensure school safety in the face of extreme events. This article proposes a tool for analyzing educational systems’ exposure, safety, and vulnerability to flood and landslide disasters across three spatial levels: river basin, municipal, and school unit. Based on the global vulnerability approach and UNESCO’s Comprehensive School Safety principles, the SAVES (Safety and Vulnerability of Educational Systems) tool proposes a hybrid index integrating school building conditions and organizational capacities. The index comprises three analytical dimensions with 34 indicators: (i) basic services dimension (BSD), measuring schools’ access to essential infrastructure; (ii) accessibility resources dimension (ARD), assessing physical accessibility features; and (iii) human resources dimension (HRD), evaluating organizational capacities through available personnel. The tool assessed schools’ exposure to floods and landslides in three municipalities within the Paraíba do Sul River Basin, Brazil. Results show that although schools have sufficient human resources to maintain daily operations, they face significant limitations in the availability of strategic professionals needed to ensure school safety during crises. Approximately 62% (n = 3,888) of schools lack accessible classrooms, revealing significant gaps in inclusive safety preparedness. Across all municipalities, many schools near risk areas showed particularly low ARD and HRD values, compounding these vulnerabilities.

items.title: Beyond “She’ll be right”: Building the Habit of Health for the Next Generation of Workplace Health
items.abstract: What if the very people responsible for protecting workplace health and safety are unintentionally standing in the way of support? WorkSafe New Zealand's 2025 Workforce Insights Programme, surveying 1,643 employers and 1,824 workers, revealed a concerning disconnect. While 88% of employers believed health and safety risks were discussed openly and helpfully, only 64% of workers agreed. This 24-percentage-point perception gap raises an uncomfortable question for health and safety professionals: Are we opening pathways to support, or becoming the gatekeepers who prevent people from accessing it? With five generations in New Zealand's workforce and increasing cultural diversity, workers communicate concerns and seek support differently. Complex reporting processes, delayed responses and assumptions about what workers need can discourage early help-seeking, allowing injuries, burnout and psychosocial risks to escalate. Drawing on Habit Health's experience in occupational health, injury management, rehabilitation and Employee Assistance Programme (EAP) services, the presentation highlights the value of early intervention. Habit Health's rehabilitation programme reported reductions in average compensation days from 147 to 56, average claim costs from $23,500 to $14,100, and return-to-work time from 238 to 118 days, alongside patient satisfaction of 9.6/10. Drawing from the success of the program while challenging traditional approaches, I introduce the G.A.T.E. framework. Through this I am encouraging health and safety professionals to: G: Give permission to speak up. A: Ask and act early when warning signs emerge. T: Tailor pathways to individual needs. E: Evidence the response and demonstrate tangible improvements. Through timely clinical intervention, accessible counselling, workplace rehabilitation and proactive occupational health support, Habit Health demonstrates how organisations can turn early warning signs into meaningful action. Every health and safety professional influences the gate. The question is whether your actions are helping people walk through it.

items.title: Beyond Operational Fluency: A Three-Tier AI Literacy Architecture for Reskilling and Upskilling in Strategic Talent Development
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) occupies two positions in talent development simultaneously: the principal driver of the reskilling imperative, obsoleting skills faster than organizations can replace them, and increasingly the instrument through which reskilling is delivered, via adaptive platforms, generated content, and automated coaching. Reskilling scholarship assumes training technology is causally independent of the skill shift it responds to, an assumption prior industrial transitions permitted but AI's shared mechanism no longer does. This conceptual paper argues that AI's dual position generates five failure modes conventional reskilling models cannot detect: velocity without capability, a deskilling loop in which the instrument reproduces the condition it was deployed to remedy, personalization that fragments collective capability, stratified access that widens the divide reskilling was meant to close, and erosion of the entry-level roles through which experiential learning occurs. Drawing on integrative reviews of AI and workers' skills, Industry 4.0 reskilling blueprints, and AI governance scholarship, the paper applies the HUMAN framework (Human Oversight, Upskilling for AI Literacy, Meaningful Augmentation, Accountability and Audit, Networked Learning) to each failure mode, and extends its upskilling principle into a three-tier AI literacy architecture, operational fluency, evaluative literacy, and complementary capability, that depreciates at rates inverse to the investment it typically attracts. The paper translates this into five testable propositions and offers implementation guidance differentiated by organizational context.

items.title: BEYOND PERSONALIZATION: METACOGNITIVE AI SCAFFOLDING FOR MULTILINGUAL LEARNERS OF ENGLISH IN INDIA
items.abstract: Integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into English language education has created new opportunitiesfor personalised, adaptive, and learner-centred instruction. However, multilingual learners in Indiaencounter distinctive challenges arising from linguistic diversity, unequal language proficiency,mother-tongue interference, and differences in educational backgrounds. Although conventional AIpowered personalisation provides individualised content and feedback, it often prioritises immediateperformance improvement rather than developing learners’ awareness of their own learning processes.To address this limitation, the present study proposes Metacognitive AI Scaffolding as an innovativepedagogical approach that moves beyond personalisation toward conscious, reflective, and selfregulated English language learning. The study examines how AI-based scaffolding can supportmultilingual learners in planning, monitoring, evaluating, and regulating their language-learningstrategies. Using a qualitative, conceptual research methodology, the study draws on existing literatureon artificial intelligence in education, metacognition, scaffolding, multilingual pedagogy, and selfregulated learning. It explores the potential of AI tools to provide reflective prompts, diagnosticfeedback, guided questioning, and adaptive learning support while recognising learners’ multilingualbackgrounds. The proposed framework seeks to reposition AI from a content-delivery mechanism toa metacognitive learning partner. Ultimately, the study contributes to an inclusive and learner-centredframework for English language education in India by strengthening learner autonomy, criticalreflection, and multilingual competence.

items.title: Beyond the tool: a systematic realist synthesis of cognitive agency in human-GenAI interaction in higher education
items.abstract: Cognitive agency concerns learners’ effortful, self-directed control over reasoning with generative AI (GenAI). Building on an existing implementation-level classification of generative AI use, this review examines how cognitive work is allocated between learners and AI tools. Following PRISMA 2020, searches of Scopus and Web of Science (2021–2025) yielded 93 peer-reviewed studies, appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. A realist synthesis specified an a priori program theory crossing the type of work offloaded (extraneous versus germane; cognitive load theory) with processing of AI output (heuristic acceptance versus analytical scrutiny; dual-process theory), and audited the evidence on each axis under manifest coding (reported evidence only) and latent coding (adding design-based inference). Under manifest coding, 21 studies were located on both axes; all four configurations occurred, two in a single study each, and the nine Cognitive Extension studies reported peripheral uses with analytical scrutiny. Of the 93 studies, 49 reported no learner behavior toward AI output, 69 reported no learning measure independent of AI assistance, and four reported processing evidence together with such a measure. Group differences or part-sample outcomes were documented in 30 studies; one further study reported stage differences, but no learner-, task-, or assessment-level moderator showed an interpretable corpus-level association with substitution. This evidence profile identifies the process and AI-independent learning measures needed to distinguish cognitive extension from cognitive substitution. The review restates the Heterogeneous Pathways of Distributed Agency (HPDA) Model as seven testable propositions and specifies the process-tracing and AI-independent outcome designs needed to test them.

items.title: Beyond the tool: what a course-aligned AI assistant reveals about student learning in microbiology
items.abstract: Course-aligned artificial intelligence (AI) tutors are increasingly offered as learning support in higher education. Beyond providing practice and feedback, they may also help teachers identify gaps in understanding across a cohort. In a second-year medical microbiology and immunology unit of 500 to 800 students, a course-aligned AI assistant built on The University of Sydney’s Cogniti platform gave students scenario-based short-answer practice with rubric-referenced feedback. Its conversation logs turned out to be a diagnostic instrument. Across more than 1300 conversations, the logs revealed cohort-level knowledge gaps and recurring terminology errors mid-semester. An exploratory analysis also found small positive correlations between practice-oriented use of the assistant and final short-answer marks, although these findings should be interpreted cautiously. The gaps were fed back to the class through an interactive revision resource used in lectures. These insights could be obtained through three approaches requiring different levels of technical expertise: the platform’s own no-code summaries, method-led coding with basic programming, and specialist computational analysis. items.title: Blending seamless and seamful tactics to nurture practical and reflexive AI competences in design education
items.abstract: The rapid integration of generative AI into design education generates tensions between innovation and pedagogy. This paper presents a pilot program that combines structured spaces for practical learning and critical reflection on generative AI. Implemented within a large undergraduate Storytelling and Animation course, the program combined seamless AI-based creative exercises with a deliberately seamful activity intended to disrupt automation and foreground human agency. By analysing student reflections collected through written reports, we find that this pedagogical program can foster diverse critical positionings, enabling students to negotiate authorship, question tool dependencies, and reappropriate creative processes. Rather than adopting or rejecting generative AI uncritically, students developed nuanced understandings of its role in their design practices. The main contribution of this work is to foreground the combination of seamless and seamful activities as a pedagogical tactic for teaching practical competences while encouraging critical reflexivity about the integration of generative AI into higher education.

items.title: Body appreciation and sport participation motivation in female athletes: the mediating role of objectified body consciousness and the moderating role of sport type (aesthetic versus non-aesthetic)
items.abstract: Introduction Female athletes train in settings where the body serves at once as an instrument of performance and as an object of evaluation. Whether body appreciation relates to the quality of sport participation motivation, and through which psychological route, remains underexamined. Drawing on objectification theory and self-determination theory, this study tested whether objectified body consciousness, operationalized as body surveillance and body shame, statistically accounts for that association, and whether the first stage of the indirect route differs between aesthetic and non-aesthetic sports. Methods Chinese female university athletes (N = 452; 201 aesthetic, 251 non-aesthetic) from six universities in Henan and Xinjiang completed the Body Appreciation Scale-2, the Objectified Body Consciousness Scale, and the intrinsic motivation subscale of the Sport Motivation Scale-II. Confirmatory factor analysis and tests of configural, metric, and scalar measurement invariance preceded the estimation of a first-stage moderated mediation model (PROCESS Model 7) with 5,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples. Results The four-factor measurement model fit acceptably, χ 2 (371) = 651.54, χ 2 /df = 1.76, CFI = 0.960, TLI = 0.956, RMSEA = 0.041, SRMR = 0.049, and invariance held across sport type (all |ΔCFI| < = 0.004). Higher body appreciation went together with higher intrinsic motivation (total B = 0.650, p < 0.001), and objectified body consciousness carried part of that association. Its negative link with body appreciation was stronger in aesthetic sports (interaction B = −0.358, p < 0.001, Δ R 2 = 0.024), giving conditional indirect associations of 0.284 [95% CI (0.200, 0.385)] and 0.100 [95% CI (0.036, 0.166)]; the index of moderated mediation was 0.185 [95% CI (0.089, 0.295)]. Two alternative orderings of the same variables fitted worse or reversed the sign pattern. Discussion Body appreciation is a relevant correlate of motivational quality in women’s sport, and the appearance-saturated climate of aesthetic disciplines merits particular applied attention. This design is cross-sectional and each category aggregates heterogeneous disciplines, so these implications remain provisional pending longitudinal and experimental verification.

items.title: Bringing Specificity to Workplace Affordances: Operationalising Learning at Work
items.abstract: In workplace learning (WPL) research, workplace affordances concern possibilities for participation and learning that arise in relation to people, work practices and their social and material arrangements. These possibilities vary across professional groups and circumstances, while learning also depends on how individuals engage in work. This article proposes a tentative framework for analysing that variation by bringing Billett’s (2001) account of co-participation into dialogue with Davis and Chouinard’s (2017) theorisation of affordances. It adapts six mechanisms – request, demand, allow, encourage, discourage and refuse – to examine how possibilities for participation are shaped in workplace practice. It also considers how perception, dexterity and legitimacy shape what is possible for different professionals and whether and how they engage. Examples from the implementation of e-health tools in Swedish primary care illustrate how a workplace change can open up participation for some professional groups while constraining it for others. The framework offers a way to analyse for whom opportunities arise, how they are encountered and under what circumstances they are taken up. It may inform future WPL research and analyses of technology implementation in practice.

items.title: Calibrated reliance on generative-AI health advice: a perspective on correctness, risk, and escalation
items.abstract: Members of the public increasingly consult generative artificial intelligence (AI) for health advice, and research has largely asked whether they trust it. Trust is the wrong yardstick. Reliance on health advice is appropriate only when it tracks whether the advice is correct and what an error would cost. We argue for an outcome standard, calibrated reliance, under which four actions (adopt, verify, reject, and escalate to professional care) are judged jointly against advice correctness and the cost of error. Drawing on trust calibration, automation bias, algorithm aversion, advice taking, and heuristic models of credibility, we read a purposive set of human-participant studies against this standard. The studies show both reliance errors. Identical advice is discounted when labeled as AI-generated, which is consistent with underreliance. Low-accuracy AI responses are rated and followed much like physicians' responses, and lay users assisted by large language models choose care dispositions no better than controls, which is consistent with overreliance. Both patterns suggest that lay reliance responds to source and fluency cues more than to correctness. Interventions that require users to act, such as verification affordances, cognitive forcing, and expressed uncertainty, show more promise than passive labels, but no study has yet manipulated correctness and graded clinical risk together while observing verification and escalation. We state five propositions with their evidential status, operational definitions, and a factorial design that would test them.

items.title: Capability Configurations and Delegation Governance for Agentic AI
items.abstract: Agentic AI (AAI) systems are a step beyond decision-support AI, where AI acts as an agent in an autonomous way for multiple steps. There are two related organizational problems: the conditions for organizational readiness for adoption, and the governance of delegated decision authority once autonomous AI agents are deployed. Based on a mixed methods Design Science Research (DSR) study, this paper reports on semi-structured interviews with four senior practitioners in the field of AI from regulated European industries as well as a quantitative survey of 302 practitioners. The findings from the empirical analysis show four organizational capability configurations related to AAI adoption: an organizational governance configuration, a graduated delegation logic, a structural governance capacity pattern, and a financial-experimentation tension. Based on the above findings, the study proposes a prescriptive artifact for readiness assessment based on Agentic AI - Agentic AI Readiness and Integration Framework (AAIRF), which consists of five dimensions: organizational capabilities, technological readiness, human factors, institutional context, and agentic dimensions. It then proposes the Agentic AI Delegation Governance Model (AADGM) to operationalize the governance of the authority shift from AI-assisted to AI-autonomous decision making, by defining task characteristics for each delegation threshold and governance mechanism. The answer to the question of governance that readiness frameworks leave unanswered is how much and on what basis to give autonomy to organizations.

items.title: Cognitive Biases in Syllogistic Reasoning: A Comparative Study of Humans and Large Language Models
items.abstract: Understanding human cognitive processes for reasoning is a key step towards developing human-level AI reasoning systems. Syllogistic reasoning — a classical form of deductive reasoning — is a well-established paradigm for investigating human reasoning, known to elicit systematic cognitive biases such as belief bias and atmosphere effects. In this study, we compare the reasoning patterns of humans and three state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs), namely GPT-4, GPT-4o and o4-mini, across multiple syllogism types with belief andatmosphere effects. Using an online questionnaire, we examine the biases in human syllogistic reasoning and compare this with the LLMs responses. We identify biases and differences in accuracy between different LLMs and humans. Belief-inconsistent statements, which contradict generally accepted common knowledge, and the atmosphere effect impact human and LLM answers. Our results show that, although LLMs outperform human participants, they exhibit human-like cognitive effects. We further evaluate the new reasoning model o4-mini, which performs nearly perfectly on the syllogism reasoning tasks and compare logic, human reasoning and LLM reasoning.

items.title: Cognitive effects of first- and third-person perspectives on navigational safety and efficiency in ship operation learning
items.abstract: Remote ship operation involves analysing information from various perspectives. However, a standardized educational approach for training remote ship operators is lacking. This study addresses the challenges posed by the cognitive attributes of individuals using remote ship operation and monitoring systems by investigating how different perspectives (first-vs. third-person) impact skill acquisition in ship operation. It introduces the ‘cognitive approach limit circle’ (CLC) concept, a decision-making criterion in ship operation, and formulate two hypotheses. The study conducted repeated ship operation trials from both perspectives in congested traffic scenarios over 100 iterations, analysing the learning trajectory regarding safety and efficiency. Accordingly, mitigating safety and efficiency inclination differences between perspectives is challenging. However, repeated exposure to ship operation experiences facilitates the acquisition of safety and efficiency skills that align with the cognitive attributes of the information utilized. Therefore, in training remote ship operators, initial emphasis on collision avoidance through exercises based on qualitative perceptual data—such as object orientation changes and distance perceived directly through retinal image alterations—rather than quantitative computer-generated information promotes the development of CLC awareness tailored to individual capabilities.

items.title: Collective Future Thinking About Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: How people imagine the future of artificial intelligence (AI) can play a significant role in shaping the development and use of AI. This study investigates collective future thinking about AI in emerging adults and factors that may influence the valence of the imagined events. Participants (N = 158) were asked to imagine, within 1 minute, as many worrying or exciting events about AI as they could that might happen in the near or distant futures. They also completed measures for their attitudes toward AI, technological readiness, and political ideology. Results showed that participants generated more worrying than exciting events for both near and distant futures. The worrying events primarily concerned ethical issues, unemployment, negative cognitive consequences of reliance on AI, and threats to humankind. items.abstract: How people imagine the future of artificial intelligence (AI) can play a significant role in shaping the development and use of AI. This study investigates collective future thinking about AI in emerging adults and factors that may influence the valence of the imagined events. Participants (N = 158) were asked to imagine, within 1 minute, as many worrying or exciting events about AI as they could that might happen in the near or distant futures. They also completed measures for their attitudes toward AI, technological readiness, and political ideology. Results showed that participants generated more worrying than exciting events for both near and distant futures. The worrying events primarily concerned ethical issues, unemployment, negative cognitive consequences of reliance on AI, and threats to humankind. Exciting events primarily involved scientific breakthroughs, increased efficiency, and assistance with learning, cognition, and well-being. Moreover, the more positive participants felt about AI and general technology, the more exciting relative to worrying events they imagined. Also, participants who self-identified as more conservative imagined more exciting relative to worrying events than those who self-identified as more liberal, and women imagined more worrying events than men. These original findings provide insights into the anticipatory process regarding AI and have societal implications for AI development and use.

items.title: Contrastive Multiclass Explanations: Exploring the Helpfulness of Class-Wise Relevance-Based Explanations
items.abstract: As AI-based decision-support systems become increasingly prevalent, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) plays a key role in enabling appropriate trust and effective human oversight. While contrastive explanations are known to support user understanding, most attribution-based methods, such as saliency maps, focus exclusively on the predicted class and do not provide insight into alternative outcomes. In this work, we propose a contrastive multiclass explanation approach that exposes feature relevance for all classes simultaneously, enabling direct comparison between competing predictions in multiclass settings. We present two instantiations of this approach: explanations for tabular data based on SHAP bar plots and for image data using RISE saliency maps. We evaluate the approach in two controlled user studies with a total of 288 participants, examining its effects on trust, confidence, and task performance. Although no overall significant effects were found across conditions, trial-level analyses and qualitative feedback indicate that contrastive multiclass explanations are perceived as more helpful and reliable in specific contexts, particularly when single-class explanations are ambiguous. These findings point to potential advantages of multiclass explanations in contexts involving multiple plausible outcomes, highlighting the need for further research on when such explanations meaningfully support human–AI collaboration.

items.title: Crisis Governance at the Joints. Mapping the Ethical and Societal Territory of Crisis Management Technologies: The Case of Human-Swarm Teaming
items.abstract: Crisis and disaster governance increasingly relies on technologies that sense, classify and act faster than humans can. Drone swarms coordinated with human operators, known as human-swarm teaming, provide a productive case to review the field of crisis governance. They promise better situational awareness in disaster response, but they also raise questions about human control, responsibility, surveillance, triage, dual use and public legitimacy. This report maps the ethical and societal territory that HST opens up. It unpacks this territory with a 3i-framework, the Interface, where operators and swarms work together, the Infrastructure, where organisations distribute tasks, decisions and blame, and the Imaginary, where law, policy and shared societal assumptions define what a crisis is and which interventions it justifies. The central claim is that these concerns cannot be addressed one level at a time. Many of the most pressing problems, such as responsibility gaps and the erosion of meaningful human control, arise at the joints between levels, through four translations, habits harden, routines become stories, principles become procedures, and procedures become prompts. Drawing on a critical review of literature across philosophy of technology, political theory, moral psychology, philosophy of mind, AI ethics, and critical disaster and security studies, the report develops this framework, illustrates it with two worked examples, and derives design and governance implications and a set of questions for developers, emergency organisations and policymakers.

items.title: Cultivating Effective Reading Habits in Higher Education: Challenges and Pathways to English Language Proficiency
items.abstract: Reading plays a fundamental role in the development of English language proficiency by enhancing vocabulary acquisition, grammatical knowledge, comprehension abilities, and critical thinking skills. Despite its importance, many university students encounter persistent challenges that hinder the development of effective reading habits and limit opportunities for meaningful language growth. This paper examines the major barriers affecting reading development among university students and explores how these challenges influence English language proficiency. Guided by Reading Engagement Theory and Self-Determination Theory, the discussion is organised around four interconnected dimensions: cognitive and affective barriers to reading development, reading culture and literacy support, literacy competence and advanced reading challenges, and pedagogical practices influencing reading engagement. The analysis suggests that reading anxiety, limited intrinsic motivation, dependence on extrinsic incentives, inadequate literacy support, vocabulary limitations, weak critical reading skills, and traditional instructional approaches collectively restrict students' reading development. Furthermore, excessive reliance on passive learning strategies and fragmented vocabulary instruction may impede learners' ability to engage deeply with texts and develop higher-order comprehension skills. The paper argues that successful reading development requires more than exposure to texts alone; it demands supportive learning environments, meaningful reading experiences, learner autonomy, and instructional approaches that promote active engagement. Strengthening reading culture, expanding opportunities for extensive reading, and fostering intrinsic motivation may contribute significantly to improved language proficiency and academic achievement. Future research should explore digital reading environments, reading engagement in multilingual contexts, technology-assisted literacy development, and the long-term effects of reading habits on language learning outcomes.

items.title: Cultural Bias and Representational Gaps in Conversational Generative AI for Mental Health: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Limited access to mental health support due to infrastructural limitations and workforce shortages has contributed to growing interest in the use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) for scalable mental health support. Despite their promise, these technologies pose risks, such as hallucinations and misalignment with local experiences of mental health challenges in the Global South. While there is growing attention to safety and harm mitigation, limited research has examined how cultural representation, linguistic coverage, and dataset provenance shape these technologies, particularly for Global South populations, and how cultural sensitivity can be improved to support mental health care. This systematic review synthesises 29 empirical studies published between 2020 and April 2026, predominantly concerning conversational GenAI for mental health. Using a keyword-based search strategy, critical narrative synthesis, and reflexive deductive thematic analysis, we examined how GenAI systems encode cultural assumptions. Our findings reveal representational gaps, limited culturally grounded narratives, and predominantly additive adaptation, whereby cultural elements are introduced while underlying Western diagnostic and therapeutic frameworks generally remain unchanged. Also, we consolidate cross-study evidence into strategies that have implications for clinical and non-clinical collaborative practices for mental health support. Lastly, we outline implications for Human-Centred AI and Computer-Supported Cooperative Work and directions for culturally grounded conversational GenAI that supports equitable mental health care.

items.title: Data-Intensive and Ai-Mediated Anticipatory Governance: A Functional Typology of Institutional Capacity, Decision-Making, and Governance of Expertise
items.abstract: Anticipatory Governance (AG) has emerged as a strategic approach for addressing uncertainty, systemic risk, and complexity in contemporary socio-technical systems. Governments and universities increasingly rely on Big Data, Data Science, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to support future-oriented public decision-making, yet the institutional and societal implications of these technologies remain conceptually fragmented. This article addresses this gap through a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) that examines how data-intensive and AI-enabled capabilities become embedded across foresight, knowledge creation, policy design, and policy assessment. Rather than treating the generic technical differences among Big Data, Data Science, and AI as the principal contribution, the study develops a functional typology that distinguishes infrastructural observation and evidentiary integration, analytical modeling and interpretation, and AI-enabled decision mediation. The review analyzes how these functions respond to uncertainty, non-linearity, interdependence, and feedback; reshape informational, analytical, and decisional capacity; and redistribute epistemic and decisional authority. The findings indicate a cumulative but non-deterministic movement from expanded observability, to analytical structuring, to increasingly mediated action. We conceptualize this movement as decisional embedding: the degree to which technological systems enter the institutional production of alternatives, prioritization, recommendation, adjustment, or execution. The contribution lies in showing that technological integration in anticipatory governance is not merely an increase in computational capability, but a reconfiguration of knowledge, judgment, responsibility, and authority. The article concludes with implications for accountable, contestable, and human-governed hybrid decision architectures.

items.title: Depth Before Breadth: Reverse-to-Forward Curriculum with Advantage Decomposition for LLM Agent
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a common approach for training large language model (LLM) agents on long-horizon tasks. However, learning from sparse terminal rewards makes credit assignment and exploration difficult. We approach these challenges through a policy-induced capability region, the set of states from which the current policy can reliably complete a task. Near its boundary, an agent may need only a few actions to reach a more solvable state, even when the goal remains distant. This reduces long-horizon learning to two coupled subproblems of reaching that state and completing the task from there. We address them with paired advantages and a progressive reverse-to-forward curriculum. The advantages provide separate signals for reaching more solvable states and completing the task from them, while the curriculum expands the capability region backward along successful reference trajectories and then into off-reference states through on-policy exploration. On ALFWorld and WebShop, our method outperforms competitive agentic RL methods at both model scales, achieving success rates of 90.1%/96.1% and 80.2%/82.6% with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct, respectively.

items.title: Designing the dialogue: A participatory study to develop AI-mediated architecture critiques
items.abstract: The pedagogy of the Architecture Design studio centers on iterative learning and critique, yet traditional review formats often induce information overload and psychosocial barriers for students. Concurrently, while artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in architectural education, its application remains largely instrumentcentric, acting as an assistant for early-stage ideation and technical optimization.This instrument-centric approach neglects AI's potential to support higher-order cognitive tasks and risks fostering passive learning. To address this gap, this study investigates how Large Language Models (LLMs) can be repositioned as active "reflection partners" to mitigate the social pressure of critiques and scaffold objective, self-regulated learning across individual self-reflection, peer-to-peer critique, and professor-led critique. Using Participatory Design (PD) methodology, this study engaged 22 architecture students in a series of co-design workshops. Participants engaged in structured ideation and created low-fidelity, paper-based wireframes simulating AI-mediated interactions. The collected artifacts and sticky-note rationales were evaluated using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings reveal that students prioritize human-centered AI features that safeguard personal agency, including robust anonymity controls, intent-alignment checking to prevent AI from becoming a rigid evaluator, and multi-stakeholder role-playing simulations. These insights informed the conceptualization of "Studioboard, " a proposed LLM-integrated platform that synthesizes peer and professor critique, translates complex terminology, and tracks curriculum-level progress over time. The study concludes that user-designed, AI-mediated critique platforms can effectively neutralize the power hierarchies and social anxieties inherent in architectural reviews.

items.title: Digital Readiness, AI Self-Efficacy and Perceptions of Generative AI among First-Year Students in a Non-STEM Language Programme
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) tools are now part of everyday university study, yet first-year students tend to enter higher education with informal, self-taught digital skills rather than structured AI training. Guided by the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) extended with AI self-efficacy, this exploratory study examined first-year non-STEM undergraduates’ digital readiness and confidence in using AI (RQ1), their perceptions of the ease of use and usefulness of GenAI (RQ2), and the relationships among digital readiness, perceived usefulness and confidence (RQ3). A purposive sample of 40 first-year students from three Social Sciences and Humanities classes at a Malaysian public university completed an online survey adapted from established instruments (α = .74–.94). Students reported high digital readiness (M = 4.19, SD = 0.49) and descriptively lower confidence in using AI (M = 3.70, SD = 0.66), with the lowest confidence in navigating AI tool interfaces and distinguishing AI-generated from human-written content (fewer than half agreed). Perceptions of usefulness (M = 3.88, SD = 0.67) and ease of use (M = 3.79, SD = 0.63) were moderately positive. Digital readiness, perceived usefulness and confidence were significantly and moderately interrelated (r = .48–.50, all p < .01), and perceived ease of use was strongly related to all three (r = .64–.68). The findings suggest that general digital readiness provides a foundation for, but does not guarantee, confident and critical use of GenAI. Structured AI literacy support early in the curriculum is recommended. Given the small single-site sample, the findings are preliminary
